analytic.title: Multi-rate DAG Scheduling Considering Communication Contention for NoC-based Embedded Many-core Processor

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Computing platforms for embedded systems are increasingly being transformed into multi/many-core platforms because embedded systems have become extensive, complex, and automated. In the case of an autonomous driving system, various applications are simultaneously running, and low power consumption and large-scale calculation are required. Many-core processors with a multiple instruction, multiple data (MIMD) architecture can meet these requirements. This paper proposes a scheduling algorithm for an automotive driving system expressed in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and we use Kalray MPPA-256 as the target many-core processor. On the basis of the architecture of Kalray MPPA-256, task processing that requires large-scale calculation and intercore communication is performed while avoiding communication contention by using a proposed grouping computational resource. In addition, we propose a scheduling method for a multi-rate DAG which is a DAG with multiple periods. This method generates a DAG task in a hyperperiod and schedules the DAG with dependency on tasks that have been released closely. The formulas for prioritization and processor selection are proposed for various generated tasks in a hyperperiod. Evaluation results show that the proposed algorithm is superior to existing DAG scheduling algorithms with regard to schedulability and deadline miss ratio.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Computing platforms that support embedded systems have been increasingly transformed into multi/many-core architectures recently because such systems have become extensive, complex, and automated [1] [2]. For example, many-core processors for embedded systems such as Kalray MPPA-256 [3] and Tilera TILE-Gx [4] are suitable for large-scale calculations. Therefore, these processors are currently the primary solutions for implementing embedded systems. Manycore processors for embedded systems can run the applications of the autonomous driving systems [5]. Generally, many-core processors are capable of running different applications simultaneously because they have a multiple instruction, multiple data (MIMD) architecture. An autonomous driving system involves a variety of different applications (i.e., localization and object recognition) that use various types of data (e.g., pointcloud cameras, a global positioning system (GPS), infrastructure-to-vehicle (I2V), and vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V)). Multiple sensor data are acquired in these applications, and they are processed by various tasks that have task dependencies. The procurement of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with an end-to-end deadline to achieve parallel distributed processing can be regarded as a real-time application of automotive systems. However, to minimize the overall scheduling length, the scheduling of a large number of tasks on multiple processors is recognized as an NP-complete optimization problem. Therefore, heuristics are used to obtain acceptable near-optimal solutions.

Most heuristic scheduling algorithms are based on list scheduling [1], [6]- [13]. List scheduling provides high-quality scheduling and is generally accepted owing to its low complexity [14]. Of particular relevance here, the prior work presented in [12] and [13] proposed DAG scheduling algorithms considering communication contention for automotive applications; however, these algorithms did not consider processing tasks that require a large amount of computation, e.g., image processing algorithms. These tasks must be processed by using separate hardware resources, such as graphics processing units and many-core processors, to ensure fast response times.

By considering these state-of-the-art and corresponding limitations, we propose a multi-rate DAG scheduling algorithm that considers task offloading while considering communication contention. Our scheduling algorithm is specifically designed for many-core Kalray MPPA-256 [3]. We divide the computational resources into several groups, and offloaded tasks are processed within the groups. Offloaded tasks are tasks that occur when the processing of one task is distributed to other cores. The links between groups are determined, and the communication between the cores is facilitated by using the links. Task offloading and intercore communication are performed by avoiding communication contention via these methods, thus improving timing predictability. In addition, we generate tasks occurring within a hyperperiod and newly define their dependencies. We also propose methods for the prioritization and processor selection of these tasks. Results show that the proposed algorithm has better evaluation factors such as schedulability and deadline miss ratio, than existing algorithms.
Contributions: Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

• We propose a task scheduling method with parallel computation that considers communication contention. The proposed method of grouping computational resources distinguishes links used for intercore communications and offloading to ensure that they do not interfere with each other's communications. The link used for intercore communication determines the communication start and end times to avoid communication contention. • We introduce a multi-rate DAG scheduling algorithm because existing studies (e.g., [12], [13]) consider a DAG scheduling algorithm that uses multiple sensors, but all sensors are assumed to have the same periods. • We demonstrate that our scheduling algorithm is better than existing algorithms regarding schedulability and deadline miss ratio. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. A system model is described in Section II. Section III introduces the proposed algorithm. Simulation results are presented in Section IV. In Section V, related work of a DAG scheduling is reviewed. Conclusions and suggestions for future work are given in Section VI.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL A. Target many-core hardware
div.p: Kalray MPPA-256 is based on an array of compute clusters (CCs) and input/output subsystems (IOSs) that are connected to network-on-chip (NoC) interfaces using a toroidal 2D topology (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2). The many-core chip of MPPA is composed of 16 CCs and four IOSs via NoC interfaces. MPPA-256 contains four IOSs: North, South, East, and West. Two pairs of IOSs organize two I/O clusters (IOCs) (Fig. 1). One CC is composed of 16 processing elements (PEs), whereas one IOS consists of 4 PEs. One CC also has the Resource Manager (RM), which manages resource allocation within the CC and communicates with other CCs and the offchip memory (DDR). 16 CCs and four IOSs are connected by NoC. As shown in Fig. 2, the CCs and IOSs are connected via NoC in torus topology and involve a low average number of hops. R0-15, R128-131, R160-163, R192-195, and R224-227 in Fig. 2 indicate the NoC routers.

div.p: An application that is used for automotive embedded systems can be represented by a DAG (left side of Fig. 3). In the figure, the sources that generate sensor data include on-board sensors (e.g., cameras, radar, and GPS systems) and external communication systems (e.g., V2V and I2V communication systems). Various applications also use stream processing results (e.g., collision warnings, automotive navigation systems, and vehicle-infrastructure cooperative turn collision caution signals). These streaming processes can be represented as shown on the right side of Fig. 3, because they can be represented by the nodes and edges of the DAG. Localization, distance calculation, and collision judgment (left side of Fig. 3) involve many tasks. The number of nodes is larger (right side of Fig. 3), and a DAG is multi-rate because it receives data from multiple periodic sensors. The deadlines of a DAG differ for each application and are given from an entry node to an exit node. Generally, a DAG is composed of a node set and a directed edge set. div.head: III. PROPOSED MANY-CORE SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: We propose an algorithm that can schedule a multi-rate DAG (i.e., a DAG with multiple periods) by focusing on communication contention and by offloading tasks with large computation time. First, we introduce an example of a DAG to be scheduled and several assumptions of the proposed scheduling algorithm. Second, we generate tasks from the nodes in a hyperperiod and define the dependencies of these tasks. Third, we explain the technique of grouping CCs to avoid communication contention and task offloading. Thereafter, list scheduling, which is a heuristic method, is facilitated on the defined DAG. Finally, We present an example schedule and explain the computational complexity of the algorithm. The notation used in Section III is shown in Table III A. Target DAG

The left of Fig. 4 shows an example of a DAG to be investigated. The numbers enclosed in rectangles near each node represent the required computation time, which is obtained when processing one PE within one CC (i.e., WCET). This factor can be obtained beforehand because it is measured offline. The blue nodes require parallel computation. The necessity of parallel computation must be confirmed by offline analysis. Intercore communication occurs when two nodes are placed on different cores. The communication time depends on the amount of data flowing on the NoC link. Hereafter, we label the node that does not require parallel computation as a non-parallel node and the node that requires parallel computation as a parallel node.

div.head: B. Scheduling algorithm assumptions
div.p: A DAG is periodic and its period is the same as the hyperperiod of sensors. The deadlines of the DAG vary for each application and are provided from the entry node to the exit node. We assume that the parallelizable percentage of parallel nodes is not 100 percent, i.e., K is not one in Amdahl's law because sending data to other cores for parallel computation is time-consuming, sequential computation is present, and result aggregation after parallel calculation is necessary. By contrast, we assume that the non-parallel node is K = 0. In the proposed algorithm, non-parallel nodes are directed to be processed by one PE because the K of a nonparallel node is zero. Meanwhile, parallel nodes are directed to be processed by many PEs in grouped CCs (discussed in Section III-D).

div.head: C. Generating jobs in a hyperperiod and redefining a dependency
div.p: Multiple jobs are generated within a hyperperiod. We must verify these jobs generations and define their dependencies. Hereafter, we call the tasks generated from one node as jobs.

First, we let the period of an entry node inherit to all nodes. A node inherits the period of the predecessor node with a large period because processing can be initiated only after completing the processing of the node with a large period among the immediate predecessors. div.head: D. Grouping compute clusters (CCs)
div.p: In this section, we explain the technique of offloading parallel jobs and communicating between cores by avoiding communication contention. The offloading of parallel nodes is performed by using all cores in the partitioned CC groups. Task offloading is performed within the partitioned CC group. Since the flow of data from other tasks can be prevented, this approach improves timing predictability. In the communication between cores, we decide the route and link between the grouped CCs and perform communication when the link is available. We propose a method to divide the 16 CCs into one, two, four, six, eight, 10, 12, 14, and 16 groups. Thereafter, we produce nine patterns of scheduling results because the optimum grouping pattern depends on the concurrency of the DAG. By using two CC groups, we explain the method of offloading a parallel job using a large number of PEs and the communication between cores using determined links.

1) Two CC groups: An example of dividing 16 CCs into two CC groups is shown in Fig. 6. The CCs painted red and green are independent computational resources. A non-parallel job is processed with a single PE (one core) in the CC at the top left of each group filled with white. By contrast, a parallel job is processed with all CCs in each group. More than two non-parallel jobs cannot be allocated simultaneously to one CC group, because interference occurs in shared memory within one CC [15]. As shown in Fig. 6, a parallel job is processed with 16 * 8 = 128 PEs (cores). Note that the red NoC links are not used. Fig. 7 shows the details of the process flow of a parallel job. We assume that the dependencies of n i,j , n k,l , and n m,n are expressed similar to that in the figure and that each job is assigned to red, red, and green CC groups, respectively. n i,j is processed by one PE in the white CC of the red CC group. Thereafter, the data are transmitted to seven CCs of the same group by using blue NoC links for parallel computation, and parallel nodes are processed by eight CCs (i.e., 16 * 8 = 128 PEs). After parallel computation is performed on each PE in the grouped CC, We use the blue NoC link again to return the data to the white CC. Finally, the result summarization process is performed in the PE of the white CC, and the parallel node offloading is completed (steps 1, 2, 3, and 4 in Fig. 7). The computation time measured offline can be used because these offload processes have no data flow from other CC groups. The required time for the NoC link communication and the result summarization correspond to 1 -K of Amdahl's law.

Intercore communication occurs when two different jobs with different CC groups are processed (step 5 in Fig. 7). The NoC link is necessary because n k,l and n m,n are assigned in different CC groups. According to [13], communication contention can be avoided by determining the links when sending data from one core to another. We also use this method to avoid communication contention by deciding the NoC link to be used for the intercore communication among CC groups. Fig. 8 shows the names of all links used in Kalray MPPA-256. As illustrated in Figs. 6 and8, we use two routes for inter-core communication without excessive hops. Let r CCsrc,CC dest x be the x-th route from CC src to CC dest and let R CCsrc,CC dest be a set of r CCsrc.CC dest x . They can be expressed as

div.p: We decide the link start and end times of these routes to avoid communication contention. Section III-F discusses the details.

2) Other CC groups: Figs. 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16 show four, six, eight, 10, 12, 14, 16, and 1 CC groups, respectively. Each colored CC in each group is an independent calculation resource. A non-parallel node is processed with a single PE (one core) in the CC at the top left of each group filled with white. By contrast, a parallel job is processed with all PEs in each colored CC group. The approach of parallel node processing is the same as that of the two groups. We use green NoC links to communicate between CC groups and blue NoC links to offload a parallel node. Two routes used for communication are determined between CCs filled with white not to occur useless hops. Note that the red NoC links are not used.

div.head: E. Task-prioritizing phase
div.p: Prioritization and processor selection are performed for nine CC group patterns, and nine schedule results are issued. In the task prioritizing phase, a laxity, which represents the margin to the deadline, is calculated recursively by traversing the task graph and is assigned to each job. Low laxity indicates that no margin is present from the deadline, and jobs with low laxity values have high priority. The equation for calculating laxity will differ depending on whether a successor job exists, whether a job has the last release, and whether a job has a deadline. The laxity is determined to ensure that a job with a small number of releases becomes smaller than a job with a large number of releases to prevent the reversal of scheduling order. Furthermore, a successor job is considered to have larger laxity than the predecessor job so that job dependency destruction can be avoided.
We define the laxity for jobs with deadlines as follows:

div.head: F. Processor-selection phase
div.p: Determining which colored CC group is allocated to the job is necessary. Hence, we access the earliest start time (EST) and earliest finish time (EFT) of each job and then allocate each job to the CC group that has the smallest EFT. The EST is calculated for each job and each colored CC group. The EST is the maximum of the following three potential values: 1) tentative release time of the target job, 2) time when the target CC group becomes available with an insertion-based policy, and 3) maximum time required for data transmission using the NoC link of a route that can be minimally transmitted by a preceding job. When the colored CC group is assigned to a job, the insertion-based policy considers all the possible idle time slots on the CC without breaking the dependency of the predecessor jobs. The idle slot that places the job is determined as follows. The idle time slot is defined as the time interval between the end and start execution times of two consecutively scheduled tasks on the CC group. For the computation time of the inserted job, the search continues until the first idle time slot with sufficient length is identified. If no idle time slot is recognized, the job is inserted after the last scheduled job on the CC group.

div.head: G. Pseudocode and algorithm complexity
div.p: The pseudocode of the proposed algorithm is presented as Algorithm 1. Regarding the time complexity of the proposed algorithm, we assume that n jobs, p CC groups, and l links exist. The computational complexity for laxity calculation is O(n 2 ) because the laxity of a job requires the laxity value of the successor jobs. Processor selection is O(2 * l * p * n 3 ). 2 represents two routes, namely, a direct and a detour route from CC src to CC dest . The maximum of l links is available in a route. The EFT is calculated for p CC groups respectively. Calculating the EST of one job requires the EST of the preceding jobs. Hence, verifying whether a dependency exists among n jobs is necessary. In addition, the insertion base policy searches for up to n idle slots. Finally, we should traverse n jobs to complete the EFT calculation. The prioritizing and the processor selection phase are performed by nine CC division patterns. Ignoring the constant, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is O(l * p * n 3 ).

div.head: IV. EVALUATIONS A. Existing algorithms
div.p: We compare the proposed algorithm with existing DAG algorithms based on list scheduling, F MHEFT algorithm [16] and HVMD CC algorithm [13] with regard to schedulability ration and deadline miss ratio. In existing algorithms, nonparallel jobs and parallel jobs are processed in the same manner as the proposed method. In addition, the NoC link used for the intercore communication is the same as the proposed method. In the HVMD CC algorithm, α which is necessary for the search of the minimum makespan is set to one.

div.head: B. Experimental metrics
div.p: The comparison of the algorithm performance is based on schedulability ratio and deadline miss ratio. We randomly generate many DAGs and determine the schedulability ratio and deadline miss ratio. The schedulability ratio indicates the number of DAGs that can be scheduled by meeting the actual release time of the job.

By contrast, the deadline miss ratio denotes the number of DAGs that cannot meet the deadline while satisfying the schedulability. The actual release time of a job is given as follows. For a job generated from an entry node with a period, the actual release time is the same as trt. For other jobs, the time is determined by the maximum processing end time of the preceding jobs and the communication time.

The deadline miss of a DAG is determined as follows. If even one job with a deadline makes a deadline miss, the DAG is assumed to have a deadline miss. The deadlines of the exit nodes are given by D(n exit ) = CriticalP ath Cost(n exit ) × (1 + α × M ) and deadlines of subtasks are given by D(n exit,j ) = D(n exit ) × (j + 1), where M is the number of jobs in a critical path and α is a margin according to a critical path and is set to [0.1, 0.3, 0.5].

div.head: C. Simulation setup
div.p: The DAGs of our experiments are generated using Task Graphs For Free (TGFF) version 3.5 [17]. TGFF can generate random DAGs for various parameters, such as the number of tasks, the number of entry nodes, and maximum in-degree and out-degree. We set the experimental parameters as follows: number of nodes = 100, number of entry nodes = [1,2,3,4], maximum in-degree = 2, and maximum out-degree = 3. The number of entry nodes is from one to four, and the number of periods also changes from one to four accordingly. Various periods of the entry nodes have two multiple types (i.e., 50 and 100). For example, when the number of periods is four, the given periods are [50,100,150,200] and [100,200,300,400]. We generate 10 patterns of DAGs for each number of nodes and periods. In addition, we randomly provide 20 patterns of execution time for one DAG. Thus, we perform evaluations of 10 (DAG patterns) * 4 (the number of periods patterns) * 2 (period value patterns) * 20 (execution time patterns)= 1,600 pattern DAGs. 30 percent of the nodes in one DAG are given as parallel nodes. The value of K, according to Amdahl's law of parallel nodes, is set to a width of 0.5 to 0.9.

div.head: D. Schedulability ratio
div.p: The variability of the schedulability ratio when the number of periods is changed is shown in Fig. 18. The values of the periods are given by multiples of 50. For α = [0.1, 0.3, 0.5], the result in Fig. 18 is obtained. When the number of periods is one, all algorithms are able to schedule jobs after the actual release time. However, when the number of periods is two, the schedulabilities of both F MHEFT and HVMD CC are remarkably reduced. These algorithms assume that they schedule a single period DAG. Therefore, they cannot schedule jobs of the multi-rate DAG after the actual release time. Specifically, the algorithms cannot consider the release time in the decision formula of the EST. When the number of periods is three or higher, the schedulability ratio of these two algorithms becomes zero. On the other hand, the proposed algorithm can always schedule a multi-rate DAG regardless of the number of periods because we consider that the job will always be scheduled after the actual release time in the proposed EST equation. The schedulability ratio when the period values are changed to multiples of 100 is shown in Fig. 19. The results are obtained similar to that shown in Fig. 18, and the proposed method can schedule a job even if the period value changes. Meanwhile, two existing algorithms impair the schedulability when the number of periods increases.

div.head: E. Deadline miss ratio
div.p: The relationship between the deadline miss ratio and the number of periods is shown in Fig. 20. The value of the period is given by a multiple of 50. α is 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 in order from the left. When the number of periods is one, the proposed algorithm can meet the deadlines because jobs with early deadlines are given high priority and scheduled first. In addition, the number of jobs to be scheduled is small (100 jobs). F MHEFT and HVMD CC algorithm give a high priority to the critical path; hence, so the priority of the exit job with the deadline close to the entry node becomes small. As the number of periods increases to two or more, the deadline miss ratio increases because the number of jobs to be scheduled increases. Two of the existing algorithms rarely meet deadlines because they do not primarily satisfy the schedulability. When the number of periods is three or more, the existing algorithms cannot meet the deadlines. By contrast, the proposed method has a DAG that can be scheduled without missing a deadline even if the number of periods increases. Thus, as the number of periods increases, the deadline miss ratio becomes high because the number of jobs generated jobs within the hyperperiod increases.

The deadline miss ratio of the deadline is dependent on the value of the given periods. Fig. 21 shows the relationship between the deadline miss ratio and the number of periods when these periods are in multiples of 100. α is 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 in order from the left. Regarding the proposed method, the computational resource will wait longer for the release of the jobs because the value of the periods becomes high. Therefore, the deadline miss ratio increases because the deadline of the job is provided according to the critical path and the number of jobs release. Nevertheless, the proposed algorithm can obtain better deadline miss rate than existing algorithms.

div.head: V. RELATED WORK
div.p: To obtain accurate and efficient scheduling, both task and message scheduling must be simultaneously considered. Table IV shows a comparison between the proposed algorithm and previous work.

Xie et al. [18] proposed HSV CC based on list scheduling in consideration of communication contention problems in heterogeneous automotive embedded systems. They assumed that the number of communication routes among different processors could differ. Therefore, they attempted to select the most appropriate communication route. Moreover, they could provide task and message synchronization, which is crucial for measuring accurate end-to-end WCETs. However, applying HSV CC to automotive data stream management systems (DSMSs) [19] is difficult owing to the following reasons. First, it does not consider processor load when assigning tasks to a processor. Second, HSV CC algorithm cannot calculate scheduling results of various task graphs. Third, HSV CC assumes that the processing time of each task is constant, and this assumption is inappropriate for automotive DSMSs.

Further, Xie et al. [16] proposed the fairness of multiple heterogeneous earliest finish time (F MHEFT) algorithm. They target scheduling problems for heterogeneous distributed embedded systems. Thus, the capabilities and links of the processors are assumed to be heterogeneous. In addition, they proposed an F MHEFT algorithm based on fairness policy by assuming that multiple DAGs have various deadlines. Tasks of each DAG are prioritized and are placed in the task priority queue. Thereafter, the task with the highest priority is removed from each queue, and processor selection is performed in descending order of the priority. Multiple DAGs are scheduled while reducing makespan because fairness policies are used. However, they do not consider that DAGs are multi-rate because they assume that multiple DAGs have only a single entry task. Unfortunately, accurate time predictability cannot be expected because they did not consider communication contention in this algorithm.

Rho et al. [12] proposed HVLB CC algorithm that can be adapted to automotive DSMSs by modifying the existing HSV CC algorithm. Furthermore, they realized the makespan shortening resulting from load balance improvement. However, applying HVLB CC to an automotive embedded system is difficult because of the following reasons. First, the possibility of missing the deadline is high when applied to automotive applications with multiple deadlines. Second, HVLB CC scheduling is restricted to various task graphs. Therefore, stream processing applications for automotive embedded systems might not be scheduled. Third, HVLB CC cannot effectively utilize resources; consequently, the makespan may become large. Finally, they did not consider a multi-rate DAG.

Nakagawa et al. [13] proposed the HVMD CC algorithm. They defined three key problems with the above HVLB CC algorithm. First, HVLB CC has difficulties in meeting multiple deadlines. Second, a schedulable DAG is limited; in this study, the task priority is reversed on nodes with rank constraints. Finally, the utilization of resources is ineffective. Many tasks are allocated to a processor with high performance; hence, the load balance of the processor is deteriorated. They noticed that these problems are caused by task priority assignment formulas and subsequently made changes. As a result, HVMD CC is shown to shorten makespan values and exceeds existing algorithms in terms of with deadline miss ratio, schedule length ratio, speedup, and load balance. However, they did not consider that a DAG is multi-rate.

Becker et al. [15] proposed a novel contention-free execution framework to execute automotive applications on Kalray MPPA-256. They mapped the AUTOSAR runnable to the core of a cluster optimally, and distinguished between the memory access phase and the execution phase. They formulated integer linear programming (ILP) to provide a time trigger schedule without overlapping conflicts. Memorycentric scheduling heuristic (MCH) was proposed, and they introduced constraints to prevent overlap between memory read and write phases. MCH has been shown to map thousands of AUTOSAR runnables in a short time without the occurrence of communication contention.

Further, Becker et al. [20] proposed a technique of dividing [16] x x HVLB CC [12] x HVMD CC [13] x x Proposed x x x x x CCs to ensure NoC links reduce communication contention on Kalray MPPA-256. CCs were divided into two groups, namely, north and south in one row. The reason for this dividing is to ensure that each CC has a private link, because it reads and writes data from DDR in IOS on the north and south. In addition, they analyzed the worst-case traversal time (WCTT) when reading and writing data of the proposed partition considering the architecture of Kalray MPPA-256. In the evaluation, they show that no NoC link contention will occur, and the proposed method will make the WCTT much smaller than when it is not divided.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper proposed a scheduling algorithm of a DAG with multiple periods considering communication contention and offloading tasks. To prevent communication contention, we proposed a method to group CCs. The routes and links among the CC groups used for intercore communication were determined. Moreover, the communication start and end times of the link were determined to avoid link contention. Offloaded tasks were processed within the CC group while avoiding communication contention. They are computed by many PEs, and communication contention of NoC links can be prevented because this technique did not allow the flow of data from other tasks within the CC group by limiting the NoC link used for offloading. We also demonstrated the approach of scheduling multi-rate DAGs and the method of generating jobs within hyperperiod and defining their dependency. It was possible to generate a schedule with polynomial time from the perspective of computational complexity. In the evaluation result, the proposed algorithm showed improvement in schedulability and deadline miss rate of the multi-rate DAG compared with the existing algorithms. In future work, we will utilize our scheduling algorithm to actual applications using Kalray MPPA-256 and schedule multiple jobs within a CC group while considering shared memory.
